entities.name: Al-Aqsa Mosque
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Al-Aqsa Mosque is the third holiest site in Islam, located on the Temple Mount (Haram al-Sharif) in Jerusalem, where Muslims believe the Prophet Muhammad was taken during the Night Journey (Isra and Mi'raj) and from where he ascended to heaven. The mosque complex, which encompasses both Al-Aqsa Mosque and the Dome of the Rock, is administered by the Jordanian Waqf and sits directly above Judaism's most sacred site — the Temple Mount — making it the most contested religious site on earth.

The original Al-Aqsa Mosque was built by the Umayyad Caliph al-Walid I (705-715 CE) on the southern end of the Haram al-Sharif. The mosque has been destroyed by earthquakes (749 CE, 1033 CE) and rebuilt multiple times. Crusaders used it as a palace (1099-1187 CE) before Saladin restored it to Islamic use. The silver dome of Al-Aqsa and the golden Dome of the Rock form the iconic Jerusalem skyline.

Al-Aqsa's political status is among the world's most explosive: Israeli sovereignty over the Temple Mount is accepted internationally, but Jordan administers Muslim sites through the Waqf. Jewish access to pray on the mount is restricted. Palestinian leaders have consistently cited Israeli encroachments on Al-Aqsa as a provocation; the 1969 arson attack by an Australian Christian, the 1996 tunnel opening riots, and Ariel Sharon's 2000 visit that triggered the Second Intifada all centered on Al-Aqsa. Hamas cited Al-Aqsa in its October 7, 2023 attack justification.
